notes.about: The spies who brought the bad report say they seemed “like grasshoppers” beside the sons of Anak. By shrinking themselves they make the giants loom larger and the land seem impossible to take. It was the talk of unbelief; Joshua and Caleb answered that the people “will be like bread for us.”

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight
figure.means: the spies' own strength made as small as can be, so that the sons of Anak seem greater still

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis, the meiosis of unbelief: the spies lessen their own stature to make the sons of Anak seem greater. Benson says fear magnified the giants till the spies felt as contemptible as insects. Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a strong Orientalism in an exaggerated report; Henry hears them as weak and daunted, painting the conquest as impossible.
notes.limit: The note does not deny that the sons of Anak were tall: Moses himself calls them “strong and tall” (Deuteronomy 9:2). The figure lies in how small the spies made themselves.

cites.quote: This is the Meiosis of unbelief. To gain credence for their words they exaggerated the size of the Anakim by lessening their own stature.

cites.quote: Thus their fear magnified these sons of Anak above measure, so that in comparison of them they thought themselves as weak and contemptible as insignificant insects.

cites.quote: They represented the conquest of it as altogether impracticable ... But nothing served their ill purpose more than a description of the giants, on whom they lay a great stress ... we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, not only little and weak, but trembling and daunted.

notes.short: A song people knew, quoted about Heshbon
notes.about: The verse brings in the opening of a song people already knew. It follows verses 25 and 26: Israel had taken Heshbon, the city of Sihon, who had won it from the king of Moab.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: Come to Heshbon, let it be rebuilt; let the city of Sihon be restored
figure.means: a known song on Heshbon, the city Sihon had won from Moab

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, among those quoted as being already in use as such, and calls the lines three strophes from a popular poem. Calvin calls it an old saying, well known; Henry, one of the country's proverbs or songs, quoted as proof that the places it names, once Moab's, had become Sihon's; Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), an extract from an Amorite song.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whose song it first was, an Amorite song boasting of conquest or a mocking call to rebuild a city Israel had destroyed, and on whether it ends at verse 28 or verse 30. It is a song of several lines, not a one-line saying.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 756
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... Three strophes are given from a popular poem, introduced by the word “wherefore.” The first ... is an ironical call to the Amorites to rebuild their city Heshbon, which Israel had destroyed (see verses 25, 26). ... The third (verse 30) is the justification of the woe pronounced in verse 29.

cites.quote: That is, an old saying, or proverbial sentence remains, and is well known.

For proof of the allegation, he refers to the authentic records of the country, for so their proverbs or songs were, one of which he quotes some passages out of ... which sufficiently proves what is vouched for, namely, [1.] That such and such places that are here named, though they had been in the possession of the Moabites, had by right of war become the dominion of Sihon king of the Amorites.
Here is given an extract from an Amorite song exultingly anticipating an extension of their conquests to Arnon. The quotation from the poem of the Amorite bard ends at Num 21:28.
